title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the two pasts and the art of insisting

questions.prompt: Four sentences are being sorted into the two columns of a grammar table. Three of them are simple past. Which one is a present perfect and belongs in the other column?

options.text: Meriam turned eighteen in October.
She has done so since she was five.
Kirsty gave up her place at college.
The family arranged a surprise party.

questions.explanation: "She has done so since she was five." is built on has plus the past participle done, and since she was five opens a period that starts in the past and reaches today: both marks of the present perfect. "Meriam turned eighteen in October." names a finished month and uses the past form turned. "Kirsty gave up her place at college." reports one finished decision with the past form gave. "The family arranged a surprise party." reports one finished event with the past form arranged. The trap is the word was: a past form after since only marks where the open period begins, and it never turns the main verb into a simple past. Always read the main verb, and has plus a participle is never a simple past. One warning, so that the page in front of you does not shake your confidence: the table in your textbook prints this very sentence in its simple past column. That is a slip of the book, and the book itself proves it: the very same sentence is already printed in the present perfect column, a few lines above. Two marks settle it — has plus a participle, and an open period after since — and neither of them can belong to a simple past.

questions.prompt: In the middle of a fund-raising speech the speaker says: "Many of you are probably thinking that a hospital as new as this one cannot possibly be short of money. The truth is that it is." What is she doing?

options.text: She is stating a counterargument and refuting it.
She is concluding her speech and bringing it to a close.
She is introducing the organisation and its key mission.
She is catching the attention of her audience with a statistic.

questions.explanation: A persuasive speech names out loud the objection the audience is already forming and then knocks it down; the first sentence gives the objection and the second denies it, so "She is stating a counterargument and refuting it." "She is catching the attention of her audience with a statistic." would need a figure, and there is not one in the two sentences; an attention hook also belongs at the opening, not in the middle. "She is concluding her speech and bringing it to a close." describes a summary and a call for action, whereas these lines open a dispute. "She is introducing the organisation and its key mission." names neither an organisation nor a mission.

questions.prompt: Read this note in a file: "The letter should have reached the association before the meeting, but it was still on my desk on Monday morning." What does the writer mean?

options.text: The letter will arrive before the next meeting.
The letter arrived in time, and it ought not to have.
The letter did not arrive in time, and it ought to have.
The letter had to be sent, and somebody has just sent it.

questions.explanation: should plus have plus a past participle names an action that was the sensible one and did not take place, and the second half of the note confirms it, since the letter was still on the desk: "The letter did not arrive in time, and it ought to have." "The letter arrived in time, and it ought not to have." is what shouldn't have reached would say, with the negative on the other side. "The letter had to be sent, and somebody has just sent it." reads the structure as a report of something done, which should have never is. "The letter will arrive before the next meeting." turns a look back at a failure into a prediction.

questions.prompt: Complete this note with the pair of forms that fits: "The neighbourhood committee ___ clothes for the mountain villages every winter since 2018. Last December it ___ eleven boxes."

options.text: collected ... has sent
collects ... sent
has collected ... has sent
has collected ... sent

questions.explanation: since 2018 opens a period that reaches today and the collecting is repeated inside it, so the first verb is a present perfect; Last December names a month that is over, and a named finished time refuses the present perfect, so the second verb is a simple past: "has collected ... sent". "collects ... sent" puts a plain present after since, which cuts the sentence off from 2018. "has collected ... has sent" gets the first verb right and then attaches a present perfect to Last December. "collected ... has sent" reverses the two tenses exactly, closing the open period and opening the closed one.

questions.prompt: A speaker wants to insist on a fact her audience is doubting. Which sentence insists correctly?

options.text: Our volunteers do work every single Sunday.
Our volunteers do worked every single Sunday.
Our volunteers do are here every single Sunday.
Our volunteers do can come every single Sunday.

questions.explanation: The emphatic do goes in front of the base verb of a simple present or a simple past that has no other auxiliary, which gives "Our volunteers do work every single Sunday." "Our volunteers do worked every single Sunday." keeps the past ending on the main verb although do has taken the tense; only a base form can follow. "Our volunteers do are here every single Sunday." adds do to be, which already carries the insistence itself: you say our volunteers ARE here. "Our volunteers do can come every single Sunday." adds do to a modal, and a modal takes the stress itself in exactly the same way.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph from a magazine. "Hend was nineteen when her aunt had the accident. She gave up her place at the nursing school in Sfax and moved into the flat next door. Her cousins come round on Saturdays, and on those evenings Hend catches up with the friends she has not seen all week. She says she will take over completely the day her uncle can no longer manage." Which statement is true?

options.text: Hend finished nursing school before she moved into the flat.
Hend has already replaced her uncle as her aunt's only carer.
Hend sees her friends on the evenings her cousins visit.
Hend's cousins moved into the flat next door with her.

questions.explanation: come round means to pay an informal visit, so the cousins visit on Saturdays, and catch up with means to meet people you have not seen for a while; the paragraph puts both on the same evenings, so "Hend sees her friends on the evenings her cousins visit." "Hend finished nursing school before she moved into the flat." misreads gave up her place, which says she abandoned the place and therefore never took it. "Hend has already replaced her uncle as her aunt's only carer." reads take over as done, but the sentence says she will take over the day her uncle can no longer manage, and that day has not come. "Hend's cousins moved into the flat next door with her." turns a Saturday visit into a move, and only Hend moves anywhere in the text.
